title: Capital Structure
subtitle: Finding the optimal mix of debt and equity
openingQuestion: Why don't businesses fund themselves with 100% debt?
openingOptions: Banks would simply refuse to lend beyond a certain leverage level
The law does not allow debt above a fixed share of assets
Too much debt raises bankruptcy risk and the cost of capital
Shareholders object to any borrowing on principle grounds
explanation: Capital structure is the ratio of debt to equity, and the optimization problem is balancing two opposing forces. Debt is cheaper than equity and gets a tax shield, so adding debt initially lowers the weighted average cost of capital. But the more debt, the greater the risk of financial distress, and that cost shows up well before actual default - in the form of suppliers tightening terms, top talent leaving, and good investment opportunities being passed up because there's no room left to borrow.

diagram.label: Debt: a tax shield but bankruptcy risk
Equity: safer but a higher cost
Optimal capital structure = the balance point

realWorldExample.description: Commercial banks typically operate with a very high D/E (8-10x) because their business model is raising deposits to lend back out, while tech companies like Google or FPT typically keep D/E very low - reflecting a fundamental difference in cash flow characteristics and collateral quality across sectors.

quiz.question: What does a D/E ratio of 2 mean?
options: Debt accounts for two-thirds of the company's total capital
Every unit of debt is matched by two separate units of equity
Every unit of equity comes with two units of debt
Total assets are exactly twice total liabilities on the balance sheet
quiz.explanation: D/E = Total Debt / Total Equity = 2 means for every 1 unit of equity, the company borrows an additional 2 units of debt. Higher D/E: higher leverage, higher risk but higher potential ROE.

quiz.question: Why shouldn't a tech startup copy the high-leverage capital structure of the banking sector, even though both are successful businesses in their own industries?
options: Because startups have intangible assets that can't be pledged as collateral
Because startups are legally not allowed to take on debt
Because banks have much lower borrowing rates than startups
Because a startup's cash flow is uncertain while a bank's is steady
quiz.explanation: The optimal capital structure always depends on industry characteristics: a leverage level that's 'safe' for one industry can be 'financial suicide' for another - which is why there's no single standard D/E formula that applies to every business.

quiz.question: Debt 1,500 billion, equity 500 billion. What are the D/E ratio and the debt-to-total-capital proportion?
options: D/E = 3.0 and debt accounts for 75% of total capital
D/E = 0.33 and debt accounts for 25% of total capital
D/E = 3.0 but debt is only 30% of total capital, mixing the two ratios
D/E = 0.75 and debt accounts for 75% of total capital
quiz.explanation: D/E = 1,500/500 = 3.0. Debt proportion = 1,500/2,000 = 75%. These two metrics are often confused: one is divided by equity, the other by total capital, and they give very different numbers.

quiz.question: Where does the optimal capital structure sit according to trade-off theory?
options: At the point where debt exactly equals equity, i.e. D/E equal to one
At the point where the tax benefit exactly balances the cost of financial distress
At the highest debt level a bank is still willing to lend against
At zero debt, because equity creates no obligation to repay
quiz.explanation: Each initial unit of debt brings a tax shield at almost no cost; past a certain threshold, bankruptcy risk starts to cost more than the tax saved. That crossing point is optimal, and it differs by industry.

quiz.question: Commercial banks have a D/E of 8-10x. Why is that level acceptable for them?
options: Because banks have large fixed assets to pledge against the debt
Because banks are fully guaranteed by the state on their loans
Because raising deposits is literally a bank's core business model
Because bank profits are more stable than any other sector in the economy
quiz.explanation: Customer deposits are debt on the balance sheet, and taking deposits to lend out is the core operation itself. Leverage here isn't a financing choice but the nature of the industry - which is why it's monitored through its own separate capital regulations.

keyTakeaways: Debt: a tax shield but higher bankruptcy risk
Optimal structure: balancing the tax shield against the cost of financial distress

practicePrompt.question: Company A funds its operations with 70% debt and 30% equity. Company B, in the same industry, funds itself with 20% debt and 80% equity. What is this difference called, and how does it affect each company's financial risk?
options: This is a difference in capital structure: A carries more financial leverage, so more risk
This is a difference in dividend policy, unrelated to the financial risk of the two companies
Both companies have the same financial risk because total capital (debt + equity) equals 100% for both
Company B is riskier than company A because it has a higher proportion of equity
practicePrompt.explanation: Capital structure = Debt / Equity ratio. Company A with 70% debt has much higher financial leverage than B - this amplifies both profit when business is good and risk when business is difficult, because the obligation to pay interest is fixed regardless of whether the company is profitable.

summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Debt: a tax shield but higher bankruptcy risk

application.title: Compare the capital structure of 2 industries
application.message: Look up the Debt/Equity ratio of a bank and a tech company, note the difference, and try to explain why each industry has its own characteristic capital structure.
application.secondary: No single capital structure is right for every industry - context decides everything.

sections.text: Capital structure answers the question: where does a business get the money to fund its operations - debt or equity - and what is the ratio between the two? This isn't a fixed number, but a continuous trade-off between benefit and risk.

D/E (Debt-to-Equity) = Total debt / Total equity. D/E = 2 means for every 1 unit of equity, the business borrows an additional 2 units of debt - total assets are funded mostly by debt. The higher the D/E, the greater the leverage: higher potential ROE when business is favorable, but sharply higher bankruptcy risk when times get tough.
Why each industry has its own characteristic capital structure

There's no single standard D/E formula that applies to every business. Commercial banks typically have very high D/E (8-10x) because their business model is raising deposits to lend back out - the cash flow and collateral (loans, mortgaged real estate) are stable and easy to value. In contrast, tech companies like Google or FPT typically keep D/E very low, because their cash flow is more uncertain and their assets are mostly intangible (patents, people, brand) - not good collateral for a bank.

left.label: High debt (high D/E)
left.text: Cheaper cost of capital thanks to the tax shield, amplified ROE when business is good, but high financial distress risk when cash flow declines - interest and principal obligations are fixed regardless of revenue.

right.label: More equity (low D/E)
right.text: Safer, more flexible during difficult times because there's no fixed obligation, but the cost of equity is usually more expensive than debt and ROE isn't amplified.

items: Industries with stable cash flow and large tangible assets (real estate, utilities, banking) typically use higher leverage
Industries with uncertain cash flow and large intangible assets (technology, pharma in the research stage) typically use less debt
Optimal capital structure is the balance point between the tax shield benefit and the cost of financial distress

lines: A leverage level that's 'safe' for one industry can be 'financial suicide' for another - always compare D/E within the same industry.
